title: Ikokore
author: Iquo Bassey
desc: Grated water yam dropped by hand in small balls into simmering stock, spaced apart and never stirred — done in about fifteen minutes, when the balls go translucent and the sauce thickens.
longDesc: Ikokore is the Ijebu dish, and it is entirely about the water yam. Peeled, washed and grated raw, salted straight away, it goes into the pot in small balls dropped from the hand with space between them so the stock can boil up around each one. You do not stir. If you need to move them you rock the pot. After about fifteen minutes the balls turn translucent and the sauce thickens, and only once they are set on the outside can a wooden spoon go anywhere near them. This is the only ikokore in the collection with a stated yield.
ingredients: 16 pieces of beef, in small chunks
// Used in the method but not listed in the original
steps: Peel, wash and grate the water yam. Add a little salt and mix. Be careful — it is slimy.
Season and steam the meat with onion, pepper, salt and beef seasoning.
When the meat is cooked, add the smoked fish, prawns and more seasoning to taste, with some more water, and cook about 3 minutes.
Add the palm oil and cook 5 minutes.
Using your hand, drop the water yam paste in small balls into the pot. Leave space between the balls so the stock can boil up and cook them.
Reduce the flame to very low to let the balls cook through. Do not stir immediately. If you need to, rock or shake the pot to free them.
When cooked, the balls are translucent and the sauce thickens. This takes about 15 minutes.
Once the balls are set on the outside you can use a wooden spoon to stir the pottage, avoiding squashing them.
Taste for salt, add the efinrin, cook 2 minutes, and it is ready.
chefTips: Salt the grated yam the moment it is grated. It stops it discolouring and it seasons from the inside.
Space the balls. Crowded together they fuse into one mass and you have lost the dish.
Rock the pot, do not stir it. That is the intermediate move between leaving it alone and breaking the balls up.
Translucent is the cue. Raw grated water yam is opaque and pale; cooked it goes glassy, and the sauce thickens at the same moment.
Water yam, not white yam. White yam will not grate to a paste and will not hold a ball — that one goes to iyan (NGA007).
Grated water yam is genuinely slippery. Grate it over a bowl and expect to lose some to your hands.
Another named source forbids stirring at any point — 'Don't mix the Ikokore when cooking at all. Just let it cook.' If you are nervous, follow that and skip step 8.
commonMistakes: Using white yam instead of water yam.
Dropping the balls touching each other.
Stirring before the balls have set.
Boiling hard instead of dropping to a very low flame.
Forgetting to salt the grated yam.
sources: Adapted from 'How to make Ikokore?', byline '1Qfoodplatter'. Quantities as printed: 1/4 medium size Water Yam, 16 pieces of Beef (small chunks), 1 cup pieces smoked Fish, 1/2 cup smoked Prawns (dressed), '11/2 cooking spoons Palm Oil' as printed, 1 table spoon chopped Effirin, dried pepper to taste, seasoning to taste, salt to taste.
YIELD — the only one found for this dish in any source consulted, as printed: 'Serves 4 small portions or 2 heavy eaters.'

The method and cues are close to verbatim, including 'Using your hand drop the water yam paste in small ball into the pot. Make sure to leave space between the balls to give enough room for the stock to boil up and cook the water yam'; 'Do not stir immediately. If need be rock or shake the pot'; and 'When cooked the balls are translucent and the sauce thickens. Takes about 15 minutes to cook though.'

QUANTITY GAP: the water yam, the central ingredient, is given only as '1/4 medium size Water Yam' — a fractional-tuber measure with no weight. LIST/METHOD MISMATCH: onion and beef seasoning are called for in the method but are not itemised in the ingredient list. Both are recorded as printed.

DISAGREEMENTS with the Vanguard version, not reconciled. Doneness: translucent balls and thickened sauce here, against 'they should float if temperature is adequate' there. Ball cook time: about 15 minutes against 10 minutes covered. Stirring: permitted here once the balls are set, forbidden outright there — 'Don't mix the Ikokore when cooking at all. Just let it cook.' Oil timing: added to the stock after the fish here, boiled with the water from the start there. Protein handling: left in the pot here, removed before the yam goes in there to prevent sticking.

The Vanguard article, 'Preparing Ikokore Delicacy (Water yam Porridge)', byline Nwafor, gives NO quantities for any ingredient — every item is bare or 'as desired' — and palm oil appears in its method but not its ingredient list. Its headnote is the better one: 'IKOKORE is an Ijebu delicacy. It is a special meal that if it is not on the menu at their party, then the ceremony is not complete.'
GAP: no source consulted specifies the grater type or the fineness of the grate.
reheating: Low heat, no stirring, with a splash of water.
healthBenefits: Water yam is high in potassium and dietary fibre.
High protein from beef, smoked fish and prawns.
Red palm oil supplies vitamin E and carotenoids.
Scent leaf carries aromatic oils with antimicrobial activity.
culturalNote: The Vanguard puts ikokore's standing plainly: it is an Ijebu delicacy, and if it is not on the menu at an Ijebu party the ceremony is not complete. The article goes further and measures its weight by comparison — for the Ijebu, ikokore carries the significance that pounded yam does for Ekiti men. Few Nigerian dishes are so tightly bound to one subgroup.
